acceptedAnswer.text: A restaurant broker or advisor helps buyers and sellers organize the commercial details of a restaurant transaction: opportunity assessment or valuation, preparation, negotiation, due diligence and closing coordination. Penthouse Advisors also helps clients navigate the connections between the restaurant lease, licensing and permitting. The work depends on the engagement; landlords, agencies and other transaction professionals retain their own responsibilities.

mainEntity.name: How do I prepare to sell a restaurant in Los Angeles?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prepare to sell a restaurant by organizing financial records, the lease and amendments, equipment ownership information, and current license and permit records. Identify unresolved issues before presenting the business to buyers. Penthouse Advisors helps Los Angeles restaurant owners assess sale readiness, consider valuation and plan a confidential marketing approach with buyer qualification and transaction coordination.

mainEntity.name: How is a restaurant valued?

acceptedAnswer.text: Restaurant valuation considers documented earnings, assets included in the sale, equipment condition, lease terms and the status of licenses and permits. An operating business and an equipment-focused asset sale may call for different approaches. Penthouse Advisors reviews these details with sellers to develop a price range that reflects the restaurant and the proposed transaction, rather than applying one universal multiple.

mainEntity.name: What happens to the lease when a restaurant is sold?

acceptedAnswer.text: The restaurant lease needs its own review during a sale. The parties should establish whether the proposed transaction involves a lease assignment or a new lease, what the existing agreement requires and what the landlord will need to evaluate. Penthouse Advisors helps coordinate these discussions alongside the business transaction so lease questions are addressed before closing decisions are made.

mainEntity.name: Can a liquor license transfer when a restaurant is sold?

acceptedAnswer.text: A liquor license may be part of a restaurant transaction, but buyers and sellers should not assume it transfers automatically with the business. The proposed transfer needs review with California ABC, and local alcohol-use approvals require separate consideration. Penthouse Advisors helps coordinate the licensing work with the broader transaction; eligibility, conditions and approval depend on the specific application and authorities involved.

When you apply for an E-2 visa at the U.S. consulate or embassy abroad, you must attend an E-2 visa interview at the consulate. If you are approved, you receive an E-2 visa stamp in your passport, which allows you to travel between the United States and other countries. The E-2 visa stamp is a physical stamp or sticker in your passport that serves as an entry document or authorization to travel to the United States. h1: The Restaurant Buyer's Due Diligence Checklist: What to Check Before You Sign
description: What to check before your deposit becomes non-refundable: financials, lease, licenses, equipment, and health department history. A buyer's due diligence checklist for LA restaurant deals.
headings: Thinking about buying, selling, or leasing?
text:
BlogThe Restaurant Buyer's Due Diligence Checklist: What to Check Before You SignBuyingThe Restaurant Buyer's Due Diligence Checklist: What to Check Before You Sign 8 min readPublished August 27, 2026By Richard Stein, COOKey TakeawaysDue diligence exists to protect your deposit: most of it should happen before your deposit becomes non-refundable.Financial records, the lease, and license status cause more failed deals than food quality or concept ever will.Always verify equipment ownership separately: leased equipment represented as owned is one of the most common surprises.Pull the Health Department's inspection history yourself; don't rely on the seller's summary of it.A business investigation isn't about finding a reason to walk away, it's about knowing exactly what you're buying.The short answerBefore you sign anything binding, verify five things: the financials tie out, the lease can actually be assigned to you on acceptable terms, the liquor license (if any) is transferable and clean, the equipment you're buying is actually owned by the seller, and the Health Department file has no open violations you're inheriting. Everything else in due diligence supports one of those five checks.Financial records24 months of POS reports, reconciled against bank deposits, not just summarized totals.Sales tax filings for the same period, cross-checked against reported revenue.Payroll records and current staffing costs, including any owner or family compensation you'll need to replace.Vendor and supplier statements, to confirm the cost of goods sold is representative of a normal month.Any outstanding loans, equipment leases, or liens against the business.If a seller can't produce clean, reconciled numbers for this period, treat that as information, not an inconvenience: it usually means either the books were never kept tightly, or there's cash activity that never made it onto the books at all. Either way, it changes how much you should trust the stated SDE.The leaseTerm remaining and any renewal options: read the actual renewal language, not just the summary.Assignment clause: what does the landlord require to approve you as the new tenant?Current rent versus market rent for the area, and any scheduled increases.Landlord estoppel certificate, confirming the lease terms as the seller has represented them.Any personal guaranty requirements the landlord will impose on you as the incoming tenant.Get an estoppel from the landlord before you're deep into escrow. It's the document that confirms, in writing, that the lease terms you've been told match what the landlord will actually honor, and it surfaces landlord-side problems (unpaid CAM charges, disputed repairs) before they become your problem. Available NowView all listings While you're researching the market, here's what Penthouse Advisors has live right now.Asset SaleRestaurant Fully Equipped, Open, Permitted Asset Sale NW corner of Westwood Blvd & Santa Monica Blvd, Los Angeles$125,000Medical / DentalTherapy & Dental Space For Lease West LA$4,800 – $5,850 / monthLicense and permit statusCurrent ABC license status: active, in good standing, and free of pending accusations or discipline.Whether the license transfer requires ABC approval of you personally (it does), and how long that typically takes for your license type.Health Department permit status and whether a change-of-ownership permit will be required.Any local Conditional Use Beverage (CUB) conditions attached to the address, separate from the state license.Building and fire department sign-offs, particularly occupancy limits and any unpermitted construction.Equipment ownershipThis is one of the most common, and most avoidable, surprises in a restaurant sale. Walk the kitchen with an itemized equipment list and confirm, piece by piece, what's owned outright versus what's financed or leased. A seller representing leased equipment as an asset you're buying, whether intentionally or by mistake, leaves you responsible for a lease payment on equipment you thought you owned free and clear.Health Department historyPull the inspection history directly from LA County Public Health rather than relying on the seller's account of it. Look specifically for repeat violations (a pattern matters more than a single incident), any red-tag closures, and whether prior corrective actions were actually closed out or just noted and left open.One more thing worth checkingAsk specifically whether the space is a second-generation restaurant build-out, and if so, confirm the hood, grease trap, and grease interceptor still pass current inspection standards. An older second-gen space can still require real money to bring current.Frequently Asked QuestionsCommon questions, answered directly.What should I check before buying a restaurant?+At minimum: 24 months of reconciled financials, the lease and its assignment terms, liquor license and permit status, equipment ownership, and the Health Department's full inspection history for the location.How long does restaurant due diligence usually take?+Most thorough due diligence runs 2–4 weeks once you have full access to records, though license and permit verification through the ABC and Health Department can extend that timeline depending on current processing times.What is a business investigation in a restaurant sale?+A business investigation is a structured pre-purchase review: pulling public records, verifying licenses and permits, and cross-checking financials, done before your deposit becomes non-refundable, so you know exactly what you're acquiring.Can I back out of a restaurant purchase after finding a problem in due diligence?+That depends entirely on how your purchase agreement and deposit terms are written. This is exactly why due diligence contingencies and deposit refundability need to be negotiated clearly in the LOI before you sign, not figured out after you find a problem.Who should I bring in to help with due diligence?+A restaurant-specific broker or advisor to coordinate the process, a CPA to review the financials, and an attorney to review the lease assignment and purchase agreement. description: Type 41 covers beer and wine only. Type 47 covers full liquor. Here's what each California ABC license actually allows, what they cost to acquire, and which one your restaurant needs.

text:
BlogType 41 vs. Type 47 Liquor License: What's the Difference?LicensingType 41 vs. Type 47 Liquor License: What's the Difference? 7 min readPublished August 27, 2026By Richard Stein, COOKey TakeawaysType 41 allows on-sale beer and wine only, at a bona fide eating place.Type 47 allows on-sale general (beer, wine, and distilled spirits) at a bona fide eating place.Both require the location to operate primarily as a restaurant, not a bar: the ABC calls this the 'bona fide eating place' requirement.Type 47 licenses generally cost more and take longer to acquire or transfer than Type 41.Some Type 47 locations carry a Conditional Use Beverage (CUB) overlay from the city that adds its own restrictions on top of the state license.The short answerA Type 41 license lets a restaurant serve beer and wine only. A Type 47 license lets a restaurant serve beer, wine, and full distilled spirits, a complete bar program. Both are 'on-sale' licenses meant for consumption on the premises, and both legally require the business to operate as a bona fide eating place, meaning food service is the primary function, not an afterthought to the bar.Type 41: on-sale beer and wine, eating placeType 41 is the right fit for concepts built around food where beer and wine round out the menu rather than drive the business: think casual dining, pizza, most fast-casual concepts, and neighborhood restaurants without a cocktail program. It's typically faster and less expensive to acquire than a Type 47, and in most parts of Los Angeles County it's easier to find available inventory for.Covers: beer, wine, and sake for on-site consumption.Does not cover: distilled spirits (vodka, whiskey, tequila, rum, gin, etc.) in any form, including in cocktails.Requires: a genuine food-service operation, the ABC can and does verify this. It's the license most full-service restaurants with a bar area want, and it's generally the more expensive and harder-to-source of the two, particularly for a restaurant that wants an already-issued license rather than applying for a new one from the ABC directly.In some Los Angeles neighborhoods, a Type 47 location also carries a Conditional Use Beverage permit (a CUB) issued by the city or county on top of the state ABC license. A CUB can layer on its own conditions: hours of operation, occupancy limits, noise mitigation, or a requirement that alcohol sales stay under a certain percentage of total sales. Buyers need to review the CUB conditions attached to a specific address, not just assume the state license tells the whole story.Type 41 vs. Type 47, side by sideWhat's served: Type 41 is beer and wine. Type 47 is beer, wine, and spirits.Typical concept fit: Type 41 is casual and fast-casual dining. schemas.headline: Type 41 vs. Type 47 Liquor License: What's the Difference?
schemas.description: Type 41 covers beer and wine only. Type 47 covers full liquor. Here's what each California ABC license actually allows, what they cost to acquire, and which one your restaurant needs.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between a Type 41 and Type 47 liquor license?

acceptedAnswer.text: Type 41 permits on-sale beer and wine only. Type 47 permits on-sale beer, wine, and full distilled spirits. Both require the business to operate primarily as a restaurant.

mainEntity.name: Can I upgrade from a Type 41 to a Type 47 later?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can't 'upgrade' a Type 41 into a Type 47. They're separate license types. You would need to acquire a Type 47 license (by transfer or new application) and hold it in place of, or alongside, your existing license, depending on your setup.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a Type 47 to serve cocktails?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Any restaurant serving distilled spirits, including in mixed cocktails, needs a Type 47 (or another full-liquor license type). A Type 41 only covers beer and wine.

mainEntity.name: What is a 'bona fide eating place' requirement?

acceptedAnswer.text: It's the ABC's requirement that a business holding a Type 41 or Type 47 operates primarily as a restaurant, with a real kitchen, a real menu, and food as the core of the business, rather than functioning as a bar that happens to serve food.

mainEntity.name: What is a CUB and does it affect my license?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Conditional Use Beverage permit is a local land-use entitlement, separate from your state ABC license, that some cities and the county require for alcohol service at a given address. It can impose its own hours, occupancy, or operating conditions on top of what the state license allows, always check whether a specific location carries one before assuming the state license tells the whole story.
